description: Elizabeth's 'Middle Way' — the Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity, and the reactions they provoked.
content_html:
The Religious Problem in 1558

When Elizabeth came to the throne in November 1558, England was a country torn by religious conflict. Henry VIII had broken with Rome in the 1530s and made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England; Edward VI’s reign had pushed England towards a more clearly Protestant settlement; and Mary I had returned England to papal obedience and burned nearly 300 Protestants. By 1558 the country had been through four different religious settlements in twenty-five years. Elizabeth needed to act swiftly and carefully to restore stability.

The religious landscape Elizabeth inherited was deeply divided. Committed Protestants (many returning from exile in Protestant Europe) wanted a thorough reformation. Many ordinary English people — especially in the north and west — remained attached to traditional Catholic practice. A significant number of Catholic clergy refused to swear loyalty to a Protestant queen. The Pope, and England’s main Catholic neighbours France and Spain, watched closely. Any settlement Elizabeth chose would alienate someone.

Elizabeth’s Aims: The ‘Middle Way’

Elizabeth’s approach to religion has been described as the Middle Way — a settlement designed to be broadly inclusive. She wanted a Church that was Protestant in its key doctrines (rejecting papal authority and the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation) but that retained enough traditional ceremony to be acceptable to moderate Catholics. Her aim was political stability rather than theological purity. Elizabeth appears to have had genuine personal religious views, but she was above all a pragmatist who wanted a peaceful kingdom.

Key Fact

Elizabeth’s religious aims were: to establish her own authority over the Church of England (replacing the Pope), and to set a uniform style of worship that most English people could accept. These aims were delivered by the Act of Supremacy and the Act of Uniformity, both passed in 1559.

The Act of Supremacy, 1559

The Act of Supremacy was passed by Parliament in April 1559. It formally re-established the English Church’s independence from Rome and gave Elizabeth the title ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church of England. Note the subtle but important distinction: Henry VIII had been ‘Supreme Head’, but Elizabeth chose ‘Supreme Governor’ — a less sweeping claim that was more acceptable to those who doubted a woman could be the spiritual head of the Church.

All clergy and royal officials were required to swear an oath recognising Elizabeth’s supremacy. Those who refused could be fined or imprisoned. Most of the Marian clergy eventually conformed, though several bishops who had served under Mary refused and were deprived of their positions. The Act effectively dismantled papal authority in England for the second time.

The Act of Uniformity, 1559

The Act of Uniformity was passed in the same month. It made attendance at Church of England services compulsory for all English people — those who absented themselves could be fined twelve pence (a significant sum for a labourer) per absence. It also introduced a revised Book of Common Prayer, based on Thomas Cranmer’s 1552 Protestant version but with key modifications designed to be more acceptable to traditional Catholics. Most notably, the words said at Communion were a composite of the 1549 and 1552 versions, allowing both Protestant and Catholic interpretations of the ceremony.

Alongside the two Acts, Elizabeth issued a set of Royal Injunctions in 1559 — detailed instructions to the clergy about how services should be conducted. These reinforced the Protestant character of the settlement: clergy were to preach in English, use the English Bible, and remove images (though the wording on images was deliberately vague). The Injunctions also created the post of ‘visitor’ — officials who would travel the country to inspect churches and ensure compliance with the settlement. Elizabeth retained some traditional features, including clerical vestments (special robes for clergy) and the use of the crucifix in the Chapel Royal, which pleased moderate traditionalists but frustrated committed Protestants who wanted a plainer form of worship.

Reactions to the Settlement

Reactions to the 1559 Settlement were mixed. Most ordinary English people accepted it — change had come so frequently that many simply went along with whatever their parish church now offered. However, several groups were unhappy. The Pope refused to recognise the settlement and eventually excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570. Catholic nobles, particularly in the north of England, retained private Catholic worship. A small number of committed Catholics, known as recusants, refused to attend Church of England services and accepted the fines.

From the Protestant side, some returning exiles felt the settlement did not go far enough. These critics — later called Puritans — wanted a plainer church, less ceremony and a presbyterian form of church government rather than bishops. They were broadly willing to work within the settlement at first, hoping to reform it from within. The settlement was therefore a genuine compromise — it pleased no one perfectly, but it provided a workable stability that survived the whole of Elizabeth’s reign.

Key Fact

Catholics who refused to attend Church of England services were called recusants and could be fined twelve pence per absence. The Pope excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570, technically releasing Catholics from obedience to her — a turning point that made recusancy a matter of political loyalty as well as personal faith.

Historians have debated the success of the 1559 Settlement. The traditional ‘Whig’ view praised it as a masterpiece of pragmatic politics, creating a broad national church. More recent revisionist historians (such as Christopher Haigh) have argued that the settlement was not a fully planned ‘Middle Way’ but a series of compromises forced upon Elizabeth by parliamentary and political pressures. What is clear is that the settlement proved durable — England did not return to religious civil war, unlike France and the Holy Roman Empire. By the end of Elizabeth’s reign in 1603, the Church of England was firmly established and its Protestant character was broadly accepted.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the Religious Settlement, always use the precise vocabulary: ‘Act of Supremacy’, ‘Act of Uniformity’, ‘recusants’. For 6-mark consequence questions, a strong answer would trace the chain: the 1559 Act of Uniformity required church attendance → Catholics who refused became recusants → this created a body of people whose loyalty was uncertain → this contributed to the Catholic threat that dominated the 1570s and 1580s. For 10-mark ‘Compare Interpretations’ questions on the settlement, focus on WHY historians differ (different sources used, different time of writing) not just what each interpretation says.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elizabeth’s Religious Settlement of 1559 was a deliberate ‘Middle Way’ — Protestant in doctrine (rejecting papal authority) but retaining some traditional ceremony to attract moderate Catholics. The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church; the Act of Uniformity made attendance compulsory and introduced a compromise Book of Common Prayer.
  • Reactions were mixed: most English people conformed; a minority of Catholics became recusants (facing fines for absence); committed Protestants (future Puritans) felt the settlement did not go far enough. The Pope refused to recognise it and eventually excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570.
  • Despite its compromises, the settlement proved durable — it survived the whole of Elizabeth’s reign and established the Church of England as a permanent feature of English life, avoiding the religious civil wars that tore apart France and Germany.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Act of Supremacy (1559).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. the Act of Supremacy gave Elizabeth the title 'Supreme Governor' of the Church of England, a more cautious claim than Henry VIII's 'Supreme Head' (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth's Religious Settlement of 1559.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor; Act of Uniformity made church attendance compulsory; twelve-pence fine for non-attendance; compromise Book of Common Prayer introduced; Royal Injunctions instructed clergy; retained clerical vestments. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Act of Uniformity (1559) for English Catholics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed chain linking the Act to outcomes, e.g. the Act made church attendance compulsory and fined absentees twelve pence per absence — this created the category of 'recusants' (Catholics who paid the fines rather than attend) whose loyalty was publicly uncertain, laying the groundwork for the Catholic threat of the 1570s. Secure: clear consequence with some evidence. Developing: relevant consequence with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Religious Settlement of 1559 for the stability of Elizabeth's reign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (established royal authority over the Church; created workable religious stability; avoided open religious war) AND over time (provided the foundation for the permanent Church of England). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a sermon preached by a bishop in 1560 praising the Religious Settlement as a godly compromise for understanding how Elizabethans responded to the settlement?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (the bishop's praise), provenance (a bishop — appointed by Elizabeth, whose authority depended on the settlement; likely to present a favourable view) and contextual knowledge (most clergy did conform; but recusants and Puritans were also real responses) to give a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source content. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The Religious Settlement of 1559 was a complete success for Elizabeth I.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (survived the whole reign; provided workable stability; avoided civil war; established Church of England permanently) AND against (displeased Puritans who wanted further reform; created recusants who were a potential security threat; Pope excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570; enforcement was uneven) before a substantiated judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: What title did the Act of Supremacy (1559) give to Elizabeth over the Church of England?
What was the fine for failing to attend Church of England services under the Act of Uniformity (1559)?
Elizabeth's religious policy is often described as the '_____ Way' because it tried to combine Protestant doctrine with traditional ceremony.
Catholics who refused to attend Church of England services were known as _____ and faced fines.
Match each element of the 1559 Religious Settlement to what it did:
right: Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church of England
Made attendance at Church of England services compulsory
Set the order and wording of all Church services as a compromise

flashcard_questions.q: What was Elizabeth I's 'Middle Way' in religion?
flashcard_questions.a: A Protestant Church of England that kept some traditional ceremony to attract moderate Catholics.

flashcard_questions.q: What title did the 1559 Act of Supremacy give Elizabeth?
flashcard_questions.a: Supreme Governor of the Church of England.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Elizabeth choose 'Supreme Governor' rather than 'Supreme Head'?
flashcard_questions.a: It was less sweeping and more acceptable to those who doubted a woman could be the Church's spiritual head.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the 1559 Act of Uniformity require?
flashcard_questions.a: Compulsory attendance at Church of England services, with a twelve-pence fine for absence.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the 1559 Book of Common Prayer?
flashcard_questions.a: A compromise prayer book combining 1549 and 1552 versions to allow both Protestant and Catholic interpretations.
Catholics who refused to attend Church of England services and paid fines rather than conform.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Pope excommunicate Elizabeth I?
The 1559 Religious Settlement was passed in which year — the first year of Elizabeth's reign?
What complaint did returning Protestant exiles (future Puritans) make about the 1559 Settlement?
flashcard_questions.a: It did not go far enough — they wanted a plainer church and presbyterian church government.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the Royal Injunctions of 1559?
flashcard_questions.a: Detailed instructions to clergy on conducting services, reinforcing the Protestant character of the settlement.

flashcard_questions.q: The Act of _____ (1559) made Elizabeth Supreme Governor; the Act of _____ made church attendance compulsory.
How long did the Elizabethan Religious Settlement last?
flashcard_questions.a: It survived Elizabeth's entire reign (1559–1603) and established the permanent Church of England.

glossary_terms.definition: Elizabeth's deliberate religious policy of creating a Church of England that was Protestant in doctrine but retained some Catholic-style ceremony, aiming to include as many English people as possible.
The 1559 law that re-established the Crown's authority over the Church of England, giving Elizabeth the title 'Supreme Governor'.
The 1559 law that made attendance at Church of England services compulsory and introduced a revised Book of Common Prayer.
The official prayer book of the Church of England; the 1559 version was a deliberate compromise between Protestant and Catholic forms.
Catholics who refused to attend Church of England services and thereby broke the law; they could be fined twelve pence per absence.
